title: Klein v. PepsiCo, Inc.
summary: The aircraft sale was binding, but available substitutes and adequate damages made specific performance inappropriate.

sections.Parties: Eugene Klein wanted a used corporate jet. Universal Jet Sales negotiated to purchase PepsiCo’s Gulfstream G-II for resale to Klein. The appeals concerned PepsiCo’s obligation to sell and the relief available through the linked transactions.
sections.Material Facts:
After inspections and negotiations, Universal accepted PepsiCo’s $4.6 million price by telex, planning a resale to Klein for $4.75 million. Earlier messages referred to a satisfactory inspection and definitive contract. Subsequent conduct included payment of a deposit, preparation and transmission of a bill of sale, review of the sales document, and an inspection at the manufacturer’s facility. Engine-blade cracks were discovered, and the district court found that PepsiCo agreed to pay for repairs. PepsiCo then withdrew the aircraft after its chairman, Donald Kendall, asked that it be withdrawn from the market.

The record did not show the absence of substitutes. Twenty-one G-IIs were on the market, including three roughly comparable planes; Universal later acquired two and offered them to Klein, who also bid on alternatives. Klein declined another G-II because prices had risen and ultimately chose a G-III. His interest was also characterized as obtaining an aircraft for resale profit.
sections.Procedural History: The district court found a contract and ordered specific performance. The Fourth Circuit in 1988 affirmed the contract finding under clear-error review, reversed the specific-performance award as an abuse of discretion, and remanded for trial on damages. The appellate court also accepted the lower court’s treatment of the statute-of-frauds, beneficiary, and rescission objections in a footnote without reproducing that reasoning.
sections.Issue: Did the parties intend to be bound before a final signature, and did this aircraft qualify for specific performance under Virginia’s UCC § 2-716?
sections.Holding: The formation finding was supported by the communications and conduct. Specific performance was unwarranted because damages could make the buyer whole and comparable aircraft were available. The remedy was remanded for damages determination.
sections.Reasoning:
The complete course of dealing supported a present agreement rather than a negotiation freely revocable until final signature. The acceptance telex, deposit, bill of sale, inspection arrangements, and admissions reinforced the finding. The agreed repairs also supported satisfaction of the inspection condition. Mere disagreement with those factual findings did not establish clear error.

The UCC’s authorization of specific performance for unique goods or other proper circumstances did not eliminate the principle that adequate damages ordinarily suffice. A used aircraft’s individual characteristics did not establish remedial uniqueness on this record. The availability of substitutes, actual alternative offers, and the buyer’s concern about rising prices all supported a monetary remedy. Increased replacement cost was a loss damages could address rather than a sufficient reason to compel transfer of the particular plane.

textbookImport.basis: Paraphrase of the exact supplied Fall 2026 Contracts Supplement; no subsequent-treatment review.

learning.why: Klein demonstrates why formation, breach, and remedy require separate analysis. It also contrasts with Walgreen’s difficult-to-measure long-term injury and Morris’s individually valued horse.

topics.assent: Conduct supports a contract despite an anticipated formal document.
topics.intent-to-be-bound: Distinguishes memorializing an existing agreement from a condition that no agreement yet exists.
topics.conditions: The repair undertaking supports satisfaction of the inspection condition.
topics.remedies: Available substitutes and adequate damages defeat the requested specific performance.

mnemonic.rationale: A Gulfstream withdrawn from the market
